baseline: On host Linux with overlayfs, chmod(file, mode) succeeds and stat(file) returns mode for all tested modes: 0000, 0007, 0070, 0700, 0777, 02777, 04777, 06777. Test passes with 32 TPASS (16 chmod + 16 stat for both file and directory variants). The correct kernel either: (1) successfully changes permissions and stat reflects the new mode, or (2) returns EPERM when the filesystem doesn't support permission changes.
failing_assertion: The test reports 16 passed and 16 failed cases. Based on the test structure (8 modes × 2 checks per mode × 2 variants = 32 checks), this indicates that all chmod() calls succeed but the subsequent stat() checks fail to see the new permissions. The test executes chmod(path, mode) which returns success, then stat(path) which returns the original permissions instead of the requested mode, causing the stat verification to fail.
root_cause: The set_mode() implementation in ExfatInode is a no-op that only returns Ok(()) without modifying any state. When chmod() is called, it invokes path.set_mode() at kernel/src/syscall/chmod.rs:81, which calls the inode's set_mode() method. For exfat inodes, this function (lines 1463-1466) contains only a comment '//Pass through' and returns Ok(()), causing chmod to succeed silently while leaving permissions unchanged. The subsequent stat() call in the test invokes mode() (line 1459-1461) which calls make_mode() that returns permissions derived from mount options (fs_fmask/fs_dmask) and the FAT readonly attribute, not from any chmod-set value.
invariant: chmod() must either successfully change the file mode (verifiable via stat) or return EPERM/ENOTSUP when the filesystem does not support UNIX permissions. A chmod() that succeeds but fails to change permissions violates POSIX semantics.
owning_layer: Filesystem implementation layer (specifically the inode operations for filesystems that don't support UNIX permissions like exfat/vfat)
linux_reference: Linux's exfat driver in fs/exfat/ does not provide a setattr callback in exfat_file_inode_operations or exfat_dir_inode_operations, which causes the VFS layer (fs/attr.c:notify_change) to return -EPERM when chmod is attempted on exfat filesystems. The Linux approach is to reject the operation at the VFS/inode layer rather than silently accepting it.
other_callers: All chmod-family syscalls (chmod, fchmod, fchmodat, fchmodat2) in kernel/src/syscall/chmod.rs call set_mode() on paths or file descriptors. Any chmod attempt on exfat (or vfat) filesystems will exhibit this bug. Other FAT-based filesystems that inherit similar inode trait implementations would also be affected. This impacts any userspace code that relies on chmod returning an error to detect unsupported operations, or that expects chmod success to mean permissions were actually changed.
suggested_direction: Return an error from set_mode() for filesystems that don't support UNIX permissions. The exfat set_mode() implementation should return Err(Error::new(Errno::EPERM)) or Errno::ENOTSUP instead of Ok(()). Alternatively, implement a capability flag in the inode trait that indicates whether the filesystem supports permission changes, and have the chmod syscall check this before calling set_mode(). The EPERM approach matches Linux's behavior and is simpler.
